summary: This document covers the CAPWAP binding for IEEE 802.11, which defines two MAC modes for wireless transmission points: Split MAC and Local MAC. It describes how the 802.11 MAC functions are divided between the access point and the controller in each mode.

plainLanguage.summary: A wireless access point and its central controller must share the work. This memo names two standard ways of dividing the jobs between them, mainly fixing who does the encryption, so equipment from different makers works together.

questions: capwap split mac vs local mac
where does 802.11 encryption happen in capwap
subtitle: A way for a wireless controller to tell an access point exactly where Wi-Fi encryption happens.

tldr.problem: In CAPWAP Split MAC mode, IEEE 802.11 encryption could sit in either the access controller or the access point, with no clear way to say which, so equipment from different vendors did not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: Two new message elements let the access point list the MAC profiles it supports and let the controller pick one, each profile placing encryption and decryption unambiguously at the WTP (profile 0) or the AC (profile 1).
tldr.outcome: Operators get a defined negotiation instead of vendor-specific configuration, and the security considerations match those of RFC 5416.

today: RFC 7494 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2015. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the IEEE 802.11 binding of CAPWAP in RFC 5416.

sections.title: The Unclear Split
sections.content:
The CAPWAP protocol supports two MAC modes of operation: Split and Local MAC, described in RFC 5415 and RFC 5416. However, some MAC functions were never clearly defined. IEEE 802.11 encryption is specified as located in either the AC or the WTP, with no clear way to negotiate where it should be.

Because different vendors defined the modes differently, many MAC-layer functions were mapped differently to the WTP or the AC. Operators therefore had to configure deployments differently depending on their vendor, and a WTP and AC from different vendors risked interoperability issues. Local MAC has no such problem because encryption is always at the WTP.

The fix introduced here is the IEEE 802.11 MAC Profile, which unambiguously specifies where the various MAC functionalities should be located.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody agreed which machine should scramble the radio messages, so each maker did it their own way and mixed equipment did not work well together.

sections.title: The Two MAC Profiles
sections.content:
A profile describes how MAC functionality is split between the WTP and the AC. Two are defined, and both resemble the Split MAC of RFC 5416 except for where encryption lives.

  • Profile 0, Split MAC with WTP encryption: IEEE 802.11 encryption and decryption are at the WTP. Because fragmentation is always done at the same entity as encryption, fragmentation and defragmentation are at the WTP too.
  • Profile 1, Split MAC with AC encryption: encryption and decryption are at the AC, so the AC also does fragmentation and defragmentation.

In both profiles the WTP handles beacon generation, probe response generation, power management and packet buffering, and queuing. The AC handles the distribution and integration services, association handling, classifying, IEEE 802.1X/EAP and RSNA key management. Scheduling differs between the two: in profile 0 it is WTP/AC, meaning the admission control part of 802.11 scheduling is on the AC while the real-time scheduling and queuing are on the WTP, but in profile 1 scheduling is at the WTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Profile 0 puts the scrambling in the access point. Profile 1 puts it in the controller. Either way, the choice is written down so both sides agree.

sections.title: Negotiating a Profile
sections.content:
The WTP tells the AC which MAC profiles it supports. This happens in either a Discovery Request message or a Join Request message. The AC then determines the appropriate profile and configures the WTP with it while configuring the WLAN.

The example exchange is a Join Request from the WTP carrying the supported profiles, a Join Response from the AC, and then an IEEE 802.11 WLAN Configuration Request from the AC carrying the IEEE 802.11 Add WLAN element and the IEEE 802.11 MAC Profile element. The WTP answers with a WLAN Configuration Response.
sections.plainLanguage: The access point says which ways it can work. The controller picks one and tells the access point to use it.

sections.title: The Two Message Elements
sections.content:
The IEEE 802.11 Supported MAC Profiles message element, type 1060, lets a WTP communicate the profiles it supports. It begins with a one-octet Num_Profiles field of at least 1, followed by that many one-octet profile values. It may appear in a Discovery Request, a Primary Discovery Request or a Join Request message.

The IEEE 802.11 MAC Profile message element, type 1061, carries a single one-octet Profile field and lets the AC configure the WTP with the chosen profile. Value 0 means Split MAC with WTP encryption and value 1 means Split MAC with AC encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: One small record holds the list of ways the access point can work. Another holds the single way the controller has chosen.

sections.title: Registries and Code Points
sections.content:
The two new message elements were registered in the existing "CAPWAP Message Element Type" registry defined in RFC 5415: IEEE 802.11 Supported MAC Profiles as 1060 and IEEE 802.11 MAC Profile as 1061.

Both elements carry a Profile field in an 8-bit namespace (0 to 255). IANA created a new subregistry, "IEEE 802.11 Split MAC Profile", under the existing "Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Parameters" registry. This RFC defines value 0 (Split MAC with WTP encryption) and value 1 (Split MAC with AC encryption); the remaining values (2 to 255) are maintained by IANA under Expert Review.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list keeps the two new records' numbers and leaves room for more ways of dividing the work to be registered later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it does not introduce any new security risks compared to RFC 5416, whose security considerations apply here as well. The negotiation messages between the WTP and the AC have origin authentication and data integrity, so an attacker cannot interfere with the messages to force a less-secure mode choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the messages are signed and cannot be altered in transit, a stranger cannot quietly force the two machines to pick the weaker way of scrambling.
